stories.brief: Chaim Topol as a major Israeli stage and screen figure whose archive documents a long performance career.

sources.title: Chaim Topol Archive
Haim Topol Archive

storyBeats: Chaim Topol built a career as a major Israeli stage and screen performer whose personal archive was later deposited for preservation and online access.
The National Library describes selected materials from the archive as available online through a collaboration with the family and institutional partners.
The archive was deposited at the Yehuda Gabay Theater Archive, indicating that his performance papers, publicity, and related documentation were gathered through theater-archive stewardship.
The National Library also records a second Topol archive entry for selected materials made digitally available with the family’s consent.
The move from private family custody toward institutional archiving changed the archive from a personal record into a searchable public research resource.
The archive’s digitization made it possible to study the span of Topol’s career through preserved stage-related materials rather than only through later recollection.

The collaborating institutions named by the National Library include the Israel Ministry of Heritage, the Harvard Library Judaica Division, the National Library of Israel, and the University of Haifa.
The archive now anchors Topol’s legacy in a preserved documentary record that can support biographical research on his work across stage and screen.

stories.brief: Ha’argaz as an Israeli industrial cooperative that began with crates and later made bus bodies and transport equipment.

sources.title: Ha'argaz
Egged's historic collection / Time Travel: Israeli Ephemera

storyBeats: Ha'argaz began in 1932 in Tel Aviv as a cooperative producing crates for the citrus industry.
The first factory opened on May 1, 1933, and the company quickly expanded to another site in Neve Shaanan later that year.
From the start, the company also brought in expertise to oversee vehicle-related production, signaling an early move beyond ordinary crate-making.
In 1936, Ha'argaz established a defense plant that produced armored and protective vehicle bodies.
That wartime-era expansion increased the scale of the operation and added more full-time workers.
In 1945, the cooperative was reorganized into a mixed structure partly owned by investors and partly by the workers' cooperative.
By 1949, the company was manufacturing jerry cans, military helmets, and logistical equipment for the new Israeli army.

The National Library’s Egged historic collection places Ha'argaz within the broader history of Israeli public transport documentation, showing how bus and transport materials became part of Israel’s industrial record.
Ha'argaz ultimately became known as a long-running Israeli transport bodyworks manufacturer, including bus production for public transport operators.

stories.brief: The Nahal Band archive captures the history of army entertainment troupes in Israeli popular culture.

sources.title: ארכיון להקת הנח"ל | פריט NNL_ARCHIVE_AL997012426841405171 | הספרייה הלאומית
ארכיון הלהקות הצבאיות | פריט NNL_ARCHIVE_AL997012426844305171 | הספרייה הלאומית
משירי להקות צה"ל| מקור ראשוני | חינוך בספרייה הלאומית

storyBeats: Before Israel was established, Jewish soldiers and volunteers already had small uniformed entertainment groups, and the archive places the roots of the military-band tradition in the wartime culture of the Yishuv.
In April 1948, the IDF cultural division created a central military band structure to unite the separate bands and entertainment teams then operating independently.
The purpose of that consolidation was administrative control and coordination, so the army could direct the troupes according to need.
The Nahal Band emerged within this larger system and became one of the best-known military entertainment troupes in Israel.
The archive description credits the Nahal Band’s early base to the army’s Guidance Command troupe and identifies the ensemble as a point of continuity with later military-band culture.
By the 1960s and into the mid-1970s, military bands reached their peak popularity and became a major part of Israeli popular culture.
In 1978, Chief of Staff Rafael Eitan ordered the military bands dissolved, including the Nahal Band.
After the 1978 dissolution, the army later restored smaller entertainment teams in 1985 rather than returning to the former large-band model.

The Nahal Band archive was deposited at the Yehuda Gabay Theater Archive and made digitally accessible through a collaboration involving the Tel Aviv-Yafo Municipality, the Ministry of Heritage, the National Library of Israel, and Harvard’s Judaica collection.
The archival collection now preserves documents, recordings, photographs, and performance materials that document how the army entertainment system developed, peaked, and was dismantled.

stories.brief: The Levant Fair as a formative trade-fair event in the visual and commercial culture of pre-state Tel Aviv.

sources.title: The Levant Fair, Tel-Aviv (Eretz Israel - Palestine)
ביתן הסתדרות העובדים הכללית בארץ–ישראל - יריד המזרח, תל־אביב (נהרס) (מבחר מייצג)
צילום אוויר של שפך הירקון, מגרש המכביה, יריד המזרח והחוף עליו נבנה נמל תל אביב
הגמל המעופף – מילים וביצועים
Preparations for the opening ceremony of the first Eastern fair in Tel Aviv

storyBeats: Before the Levant Fair became a fixed event, Tel Aviv already hosted a series of smaller trade exhibitions in the 1920s and early 1930s, building demand for a larger commercial showcase.
By the 1932 edition, the fair had adopted the name Levant Fair and was being documented as an international commerce fair in Tel Aviv.
The 1932 fair was tied to a broader push to present local production alongside foreign participation, with a Soviet pavilion among the recorded exhibits.
After the success of earlier fairs, organizers moved the project to a permanent fairground area at the northern edge of Tel Aviv, near the Yarkon estuary and the future port site.
The fair’s organizers, the company Industry and Commerce, leased land from Tel Aviv municipality and erected a large exhibition complex for the 1934 fair.
The 1934 complex included 47 pavilions and space for the productions of the Yishuv and about thirty participating countries.
The fair’s built language became an architectural showcase, with pavilions planned in the International Style and photographed as such in contemporaneous archive records.
Preparations for the opening ceremony explicitly linked the event to Tel Aviv’s 25th anniversary, indicating that the fair had become part of the city’s public celebration calendar.
The fair generated its own visual identity, including the Flying Camel emblem designed by Aryeh Elhanani, which later remained associated with the exhibition grounds.

The fairground site did not disappear after the 1930s; the location remained central to the development of the Tel Aviv Port area and later became the basis for the city’s permanent exhibition grounds.

stories.brief: Zeev Rechter and the making of modern Israeli architecture through landmark buildings and planning ideas.

sources.title: Zeev Rechter (1899-1960) | The National Library of Israel
ארכיון רכטר אדריכלים
Zeev Rechter

storyBeats: Zeev Rechter was born in 1899 and became one of the founding fathers of Israeli architecture.
In 1932, he established Rechter Architects in Tel Aviv.
The firm’s archive later entered the National Library’s online archive system through collaboration with the family and the Rechter Center for Architecture.
In 1927, Rechter designed a house for the poet Esther Raab, using an early modernist approach influenced by his time in Italy.
His work helped establish the International Style in Israel, placing him among the architects who shaped modern building culture in the country.
Among his major public commissions were Binyanei HaUma, the Tel Aviv courthouse, and the Mann Auditorium.
The archive of drawings shows that Rechter’s office also worked on large housing plans, civic buildings, and urban proposals across Israel.
The surviving archive preserves drawings, photographs, and technical documents that make his office practice and design language recoverable in detail.
Rechter died in 1960, leaving a body of work that remained central to narratives of Israeli modern architecture.

Tnuva as the major Israeli dairy cooperative that shaped milk, pricing, and food distribution.

sources.title: Tnuva Advertisement, 1930s | Primary Sources | Education at the National Library of Israel
Tnuva

storyBeats: Tnuva began in 1926 when kibbutz movement leaders decided to create cooperatives for distributing and exporting agricultural products.
The new cooperative was first organized around marketing dairy products, eggs, and fruit.
Its early public image was built through advertising that presented milk and other farm products as nationally important consumer goods.
Tnuva later expanded beyond its original dairy line into vegetables and meat.
That expansion turned Tnuva from a narrow cooperative marketing effort into a broader national food distributor.
The cooperative structure tied Tnuva closely to the kibbutz and wider agricultural movement that launched it.
Over time, Tnuva became the largest food company in Israel and came to dominate the dairy market.
The National Library primary source identifies the company as a long-running Israeli producer associated with milk, cheese, butter, eggs, fruit, vegetables, and meat.
The company’s growth made it a major actor in Israel’s food distribution system rather than only a cooperative brand.

stories.brief: The Dalia Dance Festival archive documents a folk-dance institution in Israeli cultural history.

sources.title: The Dalia Dance Festival Archive
קדמן, גורית (1897-1987)

storyBeats: Gurit Kadman initiated the Dalia Folk Dance Festival at Kibbutz Dalia as part of the early Israeli folk-dance movement.
The first festival was held in 1944, creating a formal public setting for folk-dance performance at the kibbutz.
Additional festivals followed in 1947 and 1951, showing that the event continued beyond a one-time gathering.
The first two festivals took place during the Yishuv period, before statehood, and helped shift folk dance toward an organized national cultural movement.
The festival returned in 1958 and again in 1968, extending its influence across two decades.
The performances became a model for later dance troupes, including the Karmon Israeli Dancers.
The archive notes that the festival contributed to the dissemination of Israeli folk dance and Israeli culture abroad through those troupes.
In 2019, the kibbutz archive materials were sorted, cataloged, and converted to digital media as part of the National Digital Collection of Dance Archives project.
The festival archive is now preserved and accessible online, making the Dalia conferences a documented historical sequence rather than only a remembered cultural event.

translations.ru: В архиве кибуца Далия можно увидеть, как небольшой фестиваль танца стал задокументированной историей.
translations.en: In the archive of Kibbutz Dalia, you can see how a small dance festival became a documented story.

translations.en: The Dalia archive shows how a folk-dance festival returned again and again and was preserved until today.
